title: Rakshit Kapoor
text: I’m Rakshit, originally from India, and I’ve recently moved to Vancouver to pursue the Master of Data Science at UBC. Before MDS, I worked with Interview Kickstart as a Technical Product Manager in the AI/ML space, where I worked on ML products, learner-facing initiatives, and large-scale AI applications. Outside work, I’ve also been involved in research and community building around technology and AI. Going forward, I’m hoping to deepen my skills in data science and AI, work on meaningful real-world problems, and explore opportunities.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
Starting the Master of Data Science at UBC has been quite a change from what I was used to back home in India. Orientation was a great way to get introduced to the program, meet my cohort, and finally put faces to many of the people I had only known through emails and group chats. Moving to Vancouver and settling into a completely new environment made the first few days especially exciting.
The first week of classes was definitely intense. What surprised me most was how quickly we moved from introductions into actually working with data and solving problems. Coming from a Computer Science background, I expected the technical side, but I was pleasantly surprised by how much emphasis there is on thinking about the data and the problem itself rather than simply applying a model.
A few weeks in, I am still getting used to the pace, but I am enjoying it. There is a lot to learn, and being surrounded by people from different academic and professional backgrounds has already made the experience much more interesting. I am looking forward to seeing where the next few months take me.

title: About
text:
I grew up in India and studied Computer Science at Bennett University. During my undergraduate years, I gravitated towards the intersection of technology, AI, and building things that people could actually use. Alongside my coursework, I spent a lot of time working on machine learning projects, experimenting with different applications of AI, and getting involved in student communities.
Before starting the MDS program, I worked at Interview Kickstart in the AI/ML space. My work there sat somewhere between technology, product development, and education, which gave me the chance to work with both technical problems and people. I particularly enjoyed working on AI-powered applications and figuring out how to turn fairly complex technical ideas into something useful and accessible.

title: About
text:
Why data science
My interest in data science grew from wanting to understand not just how models work, but how data can be used to make better decisions and solve problems in the real world. I have worked with machine learning and deep learning through projects and research, but I wanted a stronger foundation across statistics, data analysis, and the broader data science workflow.
That is what brought me to UBC’s Master of Data Science. I am particularly interested in the space where machine learning, AI, and practical problem-solving meet. I am hoping to use the program to become better at taking a problem from messy data all the way to a useful, well-reasoned solution.

title: About
text:
Outside of data science
Outside of work and academics, I enjoy being around people and building communities. During university, I was involved in running a student technology club, which meant organising workshops, bringing people together, and occasionally figuring out how to make ambitious ideas happen with very limited resources.
I also enjoy exploring new places, trying different food, and finding good coffee spots. Now that I am in Vancouver, I am looking forward to doing a lot more of that, whether it is exploring the city, discovering new trails, or simply finding a favourite neighbourhood spot. I am also a big fan of conversations that have absolutely nothing to do with data science.

title: Exploring Penguin Size
text:
In this post, I explore the relationship between penguin body mass and flipper length across three penguin species: Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo. I use Python to calculate summary statistics, visualize the relationship between measurements, and compare average body mass across species.
The data come from the Palmer Penguins dataset, collected by Dr. Kristen Gorman and the Palmer Station Antarctica LTER. The dataset is available through the palmerpenguins Python package.

title: Exploring Penguin Size
text:
In this post, I explore the relationship between penguin body mass and flipper length across three penguin species: Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo. I use Python to calculate summary statistics, visualize the relationship between measurements, and compare average body mass across species.
The data come from the Palmer Penguins dataset, collected by Dr. Kristen Gorman and the Palmer Station Antarctica LTER. The dataset is available through the palmerpenguins Python package.

title: Exploring Penguin Size
text:
2. Compare penguin size by species
Next, I calculate the average body mass and flipper length for each species. Missing measurements are excluded from the calculations.

species_summary = (
    penguins
    .groupby("species")[["body_mass_g", "flipper_length_mm"]]
    .mean()
    .round(2)
)

title: Exploring Penguin Size
section: 3. Visualize body mass and flipper length
text:
3. Visualize body mass and flipper length
I use a scatter plot to investigate the relationship between flipper length and body mass. Each species is represented separately to make comparisons easier.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 6))

for species in penguins["species"].dropna().unique():
    subset = penguins[
        penguins["species"] == species
    ]

    ax.scatter(
        subset["flipper_length_mm"],
        subset["body_mass_g"],
        label=species,
        alpha=0.7
    )

ax.set_xlabel("Flipper length (mm)")
ax.set_ylabel("Body mass (g)")
ax.set_title("Penguin Body Mass vs Flipper Length")
ax.legend(title="Species")
ax.grid(alpha=0.2)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1: Relationship between flipper length and body mass across three penguin species.





The scatter plot illustrates a positive association between flipper length and body mass. Penguins with longer flippers generally have greater body mass, although the measurements vary within each species.

title: Exploring Penguin Size
section: 4. Identify the species with the largest average body mass
text:
4. Identify the species with the largest average body mass
Finally, I use the summary statistics to identify which species has the largest average body mass.

largest_species = species_summary["body_mass_g"].idxmax()

largest_mass = species_summary["body_mass_g"].max()

print(
    f"{largest_species} has the largest average "
    f"body mass: {largest_mass:.2f} g."
)

Gentoo has the largest average body mass: 5076.02 g.


This calculation provides a direct comparison of average body mass across the three species.

title: Exploring Penguin Size
text:
Conclusion
The analysis demonstrates how Python can be used to explore and summarize biological measurements. The species-level statistics show differences in average body mass and flipper length, while the scatter plot reveals a positive relationship between these measurements.
Gentoo penguins have the largest average body mass among the three species in this dataset. The analysis also demonstrates how grouping, aggregation, and visualization can help identify patterns in real-world data.
